question: A blood donor's serology shows: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM negative, anti-HBc IgG positive, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, HBV DNA 500 IU/mL. What is the most likely interpretation?

answers.text: Inactive HBsAg carrier — past seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe with suppressed viral replication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. HBsAg positive (chronic infection) + anti-HBc IgG positive (long-standing) + IgM negative (not acute) + HBeAg negative/anti-HBe positive (seroconverted) + low DNA = inactive carrier. The immune system has controlled replication but not cleared the surface antigen.

answers.text: Acute hepatitis B infection in the early phase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acute HBV requires anti-HBc IgM positivity — the hallmark of recent infection. This donor has IgM negative and IgG positive, indicating chronic (long-standing) infection, not acute.
Vaccination produces ONLY anti-HBs — never HBsAg, never anti-HBc. The presence of HBsAg and anti-HBc here confirms natural infection, not vaccination.

answers.text: Window period of resolving acute HBV infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Window period is defined by: HBsAg cleared + anti-HBs not yet appeared + anti-HBc IgM as the sole marker. This donor has HBsAg PRESENT — completely ruling out the window period.

overallFeedback.feedback: Interpret systematically: HBsAg (infection status) → IgM vs IgG (acute vs chronic) → HBeAg/anti-HBe (replication status) → DNA (viral load). This combination = inactive carrier.
Inactive carrier: HBsAg+ / anti-HBe+ / low DNA. The donor has controlled but not eliminated HBV — still a blood-bank exclusion.
